analogy.p: An image is like a mosaic made of square tiles. Each tile is a pixel and can only be one colour. The number of tiles across and down is the resolution: more tiles of smaller size give a finer, more detailed picture. The colour depth is how many different colours of tile are in the tile box: with 2 colours you can make only a black and white picture, but with millions of colours you can get smooth photos. A bigger mosaic with more colours needs more tiles and a longer instruction sheet to rebuild it, which is like a larger file size, and the instruction sheet's first line stating the size of the mosaic and number of colours is the metadata. The analogy breaks down because a real mosaic tile is a physical object, whereas a pixel is just a binary number that a screen turns into light, and the bits used per pixel can be changed without changing the size of the picture.

bullets: A **pixel** is the smallest single element of an image; each pixel has **one** colour.
An image is stored as a **grid** of pixels arranged in rows and columns, read from the top left, row by row.
Each pixel's colour is stored as a **binary code**.
The more pixels there are, the more accurately the original picture is captured.
When you zoom in far enough, you see the **individual pixels** as coloured squares (pixelation).
Bitmap images are made of pixels; this is the type of image the OCR J277 specification asks you to know.
Photos from a camera, screenshots and most web images are bitmaps.
core.p: A digital image on a computer is stored as a **bitmap**: a grid of tiny squares called **pixels** (short for picture elements). Each pixel is a single block of one solid colour, and when thousands or millions of pixels are placed side by side, your eyes blend them into a smooth picture. A computer cannot store a picture directly, so it breaks the picture into a grid and stores the colour of every pixel as a **binary number**. To display the image, the computer reads the numbers in order, works out each pixel's colour and draws the grid on screen. That is why zooming in on a digital photo eventually shows individual coloured squares.

bullets: With **1 bit** per pixel there are only 2 possible values: 0 and 1, so only **2 colours**.
You must be told the **meaning** of each value, for example 1 = black, 0 = white.
Read the pixels **left to right**, then move to the next row down.
Example row 00111100 means 2 white, 4 black, 2 white pixels.
An 8 x 8 image has 64 pixels, so **64 bits** = 64 / 8 = **8 bytes**.
Exam tip: when drawing from binary, split the long binary string into rows of the **image width**.
To convert a picture to binary, shade the pixels and write 1 for shaded and 0 for blank.
core.h: Storing a pixel in binary: the 1-bit image
core.p: The simplest possible image uses only **two colours**, such as black and white. Two colours need only **one bit** per pixel, so we can say 0 is white and 1 is black. A black and white image of 8 pixels by 8 pixels needs 64 bits (8 bytes) of pixel data. To store it, we write down the bit for each pixel row by row from the top left. To rebuild it, the computer lays out the bits in rows of the correct width and colours each square. Being able to read a grid of 1s and 0s and draw the picture (or the reverse) is a standard exam skill.

bullets: Colour depth = **bits per pixel**.
**Increase colour depth by 1 bit and the number of colours doubles.**
To find the colour depth needed for a given number of colours, find the smallest n with 2^n at least that number: 40 colours needs 6 bits (2^5 = 32 is too few, 2^6 = 64 is enough).
Low colour depth gives visible **bands** or blocks of colour where smooth shading should be.
Higher colour depth = **better quality** but **bigger file size**.
Colour depth is stored in the file's **metadata**.
core.p: **Colour depth** is the **number of bits used to represent the colour of each pixel**. The bigger the colour depth, the more different colours the image can use, because n bits can make 2^n different binary patterns. One bit gives 2 colours, 2 bits give 4 colours, 4 bits give 16, 8 bits give 256 and 24 bits give over 16 million. Every extra bit **doubles** the number of colours. A higher colour depth makes the image look more realistic with smoother changes in shade, but every pixel needs more bits, so the file becomes larger.

bullets: A **palette** matches each binary code to a colour, so fewer bits are needed per pixel.
2-bit example: 00 = white, 01 = black, 10 = red, 11 = blue; the pixel code 10 is drawn as red.
RGB: colours are made by mixing **red, green and blue** light in different amounts.
In 24-bit colour each of R, G and B has **8 bits** (0 to 255); (255, 0, 0) is pure red.
8 bits x 3 colours = **24 bits per pixel**; 2^24 = about **16.7 million** colours.
Black is (0, 0, 0) and white is (255, 255, 255) in 24-bit RGB.
You will be told the colour code meaning in an exam; you do not need to learn palettes.
core.p: With a small colour depth, each binary code can be linked to a colour in a **palette** (a table). For example, with 2 bits: 00 = white, 01 = black, 10 = red, 11 = blue. The computer stores only the 2-bit codes and uses the table to find each colour. For realistic photos, screens use the **RGB** model: each pixel is a mix of red, green and blue light. In a **24-bit** image, 8 bits are used for each of the three colours, so each can have 256 levels (0 to 255), giving 256 x 256 x 256 = 16,777,216 colours. Each pixel therefore needs 24 bits (3 bytes).

bullets: Resolution = **width in pixels x height in pixels**, for example 800 x 600 = 480,000 pixels.
More pixels give **more detail** and a sharper picture.
Fewer pixels give a **blocky (pixelated)** image, especially when enlarged.
Doubling both width and height gives **4 times** as many pixels.
Higher resolution means **more bits to store**, so a bigger file size.
Resolution is also stored in the file's **metadata**.
Do not mix up resolution (number of pixels) with colour depth (bits per pixel).
core.p: **Resolution** is the **number of pixels** in an image, normally given as the width in pixels by the height in pixels, such as 1920 x 1080. Total pixels = width x height. A higher resolution means more, smaller pixels, so the image captures more detail and looks sharper when enlarged. A lower resolution has fewer, larger pixels and looks blocky. Higher resolution also needs more data, because every extra pixel has to be stored. Resolution is the second factor, with colour depth, that decides the quality and the file size of an image.

bullets: Higher **resolution** = more pixels = more detail **and** a larger file.
Higher **colour depth** = more possible colours = more realistic colours **and** a larger file.
File size is proportional to **both**: change one factor by x and the size changes by x.
8-bit to 24-bit colour makes the file **3 times** bigger (24 / 8 = 3).
Halving width and height gives **a quarter** of the pixels and a quarter of the file size.
Larger files need **more storage** and take **longer to upload, download and process**.
Designers choose a **balance** between quality and size: small web images use lower settings; print photos use higher.
core.h: How resolution and colour depth affect quality and file size
core.p: Both factors work in the same direction: raising either one improves the quality and increases the file size, and lowering either shrinks the file but loses quality. Because file size is **width x height x colour depth**, file size is directly proportional to each factor. Doubling the colour depth (for example 8 to 16 bits) doubles the file size; tripling it (8 to 24 bits) triples it. Doubling the width only doubles the pixels, but doubling width and height multiplies the pixels (and size) by 4. Exam answers need this link between the factor, the quality and the size.

bullets: Step 1: pixels = **width x height**.
Step 2: bits = pixels x **colour depth**.
Step 3: bytes = bits / **8**.
Step 4: kilobytes = bytes / **1000**; megabytes = kilobytes / 1000.
Example: 100 x 50 pixels at 8 bits = 5000 x 8 = 40,000 bits = **5000 bytes = 5 kB**.
Reverse questions: to find colour depth, divide the file size in bits by the number of pixels.
Always **show your working** and give **units**.
core.h: Calculating the size of an image file
core.p: The file size calculation is the key numerical skill for this topic. The formula is **file size (bits) = width (pixels) x height (pixels) x colour depth (bits)**. This gives bits; to give the answer in other units, divide by 8 for bytes, then by 1000 for kilobytes (OCR uses 1 kB = 1000 bytes) and by 1000 again for megabytes. Write each step, because the mark scheme gives marks for finding the number of pixels, multiplying by colour depth, and converting units. Include the metadata only if the question says to; usually you are asked for the pixel data only.

bullets: Metadata = **data about the data** in a file.
Essential image metadata: **width, height (resolution) and colour depth**.
Other metadata: **file format**, **date and time created**, **camera or device model**, **GPS location**, exposure settings, file size.
Without width and height the computer cannot work out where each row **ends**.
Metadata takes extra storage, so a file is slightly **bigger than the pixel data alone**.
Metadata can raise **privacy** concerns: a photo shared online may reveal where and when it was taken.
Metadata can be used to **search, sort and organise** images, for example finding all photos taken on a date.
core.p: **Metadata** is data about data: extra information stored in an image file in addition to the pixel colours. The computer needs some of it to rebuild the picture; for instance, the stream of bits 0110100110010110 could be a 4 x 4 grid, a 2 x 8 grid or an 8 x 2 grid, so the **width and height** must be stored. The **colour depth** must also be stored so the computer knows how many bits make up each pixel. Other metadata is useful for people and software, such as the date the picture was taken, the camera or phone model, the GPS location and the file format. Metadata is stored in a **header** at the start of the file.

bullets: Worked decode: width 4, 1 bit, string 0110 1001 1001 0110 gives a ring shape (1 = black).
For **2-bit colour**, first split into pairs: 00 01 10 11 ... then arrange the pairs into rows of the width.
If the width is 6 pixels at 2 bits, each row has 6 x 2 = **12 bits**.
Check that the total bits = **width x height x colour depth**; if not, you have miscounted.
Draw each pixel using the **key** given in the question.
Use a ruler and neat squares; label rows if helpful.
Marks are for **correct row order**, correct pixel colours and correct total number of pixels.
core.h: Reading and drawing bitmap images from binary
core.p: Exam questions often give you a binary string or a grid and ask you to convert between them. The method is to use the **width** to break the stream into rows, then use the **colour key** to colour each pixel. For multi-bit pixels, the stream has to be split into groups of the colour depth first, and then the groups are arranged into rows. Take care to count carefully, because one missing bit shifts every following pixel. When writing binary from a picture, go row by row from the top left, writing pixels left to right.

bullets: Large files need **more storage capacity** and **more memory** to open and edit.
Large files take **longer to download or upload** and use more **bandwidth**.
Reducing resolution or colour depth reduces size but also **quality**.
The right setting depends on the use: **web thumbnails** versus **large print**.
Images can also be **compressed** (lossy or lossless) to reduce size without changing resolution.
Lossy compression permanently removes some data; lossless keeps all of it but compresses less.
Choose and justify: 'I would use a lower resolution because the image is only shown on a small screen, which makes the file smaller and quicker to load.'
core.h: Why quality and size must be balanced
core.p: There is always a trade-off. A high resolution, high colour depth image looks excellent but may be several megabytes. Storing thousands of them needs a lot of **storage space**, and sending or downloading them uses **bandwidth** and takes time. A website with huge images loads slowly, and mobile users may use up their data allowance. A small, low-quality image saves space but looks blocky or lacks colour. Compression reduces file size, and so does choosing a sensible resolution and colour depth for the purpose. A suitable choice depends on the use: a profile picture needs far fewer pixels than a poster.

bullets: **Text**: bits per character determines how many characters; **colour depth** is the same rule for colours.
**Sound**: sample rate and bit depth also trade quality against file size.
**Units and storage**: bits to bytes to kB uses the same conversions.
**Compression**: lossy methods such as JPEG reduce image size; lossless methods such as PNG keep all the data.
**Networks**: larger images need more bandwidth and take longer to transmit.
**Binary conversion**: you use binary to denary skills to read pixel codes.
**Ethics and privacy**: image metadata such as location can be a privacy risk.
core.p: Images are one of three main data types (with text and sound) that you must be able to represent in binary. The same idea of **bits determine possibilities, and more bits means a bigger file** links colour depth to ASCII and Unicode (bits per character) and to sound bit depth. The size calculation uses the **units** (bits, bytes, kB, MB) and the same binary skills. **Compression** is a direct follow-on, as images are the data most often compressed. Finally, image data travels over **networks**, so image size affects speed and costs.

bullets: Always say **what** you would change, **what effect** it has on quality, and **what effect** on file size.
A large poster needs a **high resolution**, otherwise pixels become visible when it is enlarged.
A simple logo with 4 colours only needs **2 bits** per pixel, not 24.
Reducing 24-bit to 8-bit colour cuts the file to **one third**, but may cause banding.
Consider the **device**: a phone screen shows fewer pixels than a large TV.
Consider the **connection**: slow connections need smaller files.
Consider **purpose**: archive photos need quality; thumbnails need small size.
core.h: Higher-level extension: comparing images and designing settings
core.p: Longer questions may present a scenario, such as a website designer or a photographer, and ask you to recommend settings. The best answers state the settings, then link each to quality **and** to file size, and then to the context. For example, a photographer who wants large prints needs a high resolution and a high colour depth so detail and colour are accurate, accepting large files and needing big storage. A designer making a quick-loading icon for a website would use a small resolution and fewer colours, as the viewer does not need fine detail, and the file loads quickly on slow connections.

exam: **State/Give (1 mark)**: 'Resolution is the number of pixels in an image' or 'Colour depth is the number of bits used for each pixel'. One short, accurate fact.

**Describe how an image is stored (2 to 3 marks)**: the image is made of a grid of pixels; each pixel is given a binary value for its colour; the values are stored in order along with metadata such as width and height.
**Explain the effect of increasing colour depth (2 marks)**: more bits per pixel, so more colours can be shown / better quality (1); each pixel needs more bits so the file size is larger (1).
**Explain the effect of increasing resolution (2 marks)**: more pixels, so more detail/sharper (1); more data to store so a larger file (1).
**Calculation (3 to 4 marks)**: width x height (1), x colour depth (1), / 8 to bytes (1), correct final unit (1). Show every step and write the unit.
**'How many colours?'**: use 2^bits, for example 2^8 = 256. For 'bits needed', choose the smallest power of 2 big enough (for 100 colours, 7 bits).
**Metadata questions (1 to 2 marks)**: define it as data about the data (1) and give examples: width, height, colour depth, date, location, camera model (1 each, usually max 2 or 3).
**Why is metadata needed?**: the computer needs the width/height to know where each row ends and colour depth to know how many bits per pixel, so it can rebuild the image.
**Drawing from binary**: split the string into rows of the given width; apply the colour key; check your total pixels equal width x height; neat shaded squares.
**Six-mark questions**: balance quality and file size, give consequences (storage, download time) and relate settings to the context; finish with a justified conclusion.
**Avoid** vague wording like 'better picture' or 'takes more space' without saying why: link back to pixels or bits per pixel.

mistakes.r: Resolution is the number of pixels in the image (width x height); more pixels means more detail.
mistakes.w: Saying resolution is how clear the picture is, with no mention of pixels.

mistakes.r: Colour depth is the number of bits per pixel (how many colours); resolution is the number of pixels.
mistakes.w: Mixing up colour depth and resolution.

mistakes.r: File size in bits = width x height x colour depth; divide by 8 for bytes.
mistakes.w: Forgetting to divide by 8 to get bytes.

mistakes.r: In OCR J277, 1 kilobyte = 1000 bytes; use the conversions given by the board.
mistakes.w: Using 1024 when OCR expects 1000 for kilobytes.

mistakes.r: A higher colour depth means more bits per pixel, so more possible colours, not more pixels.
mistakes.w: Saying a higher colour depth means more pixels.

mistakes.r: Metadata is data about the image, such as width, height, colour depth, file type and date; the pixel colours are the image data.
mistakes.w: Saying metadata is the pixel colours themselves.

mistakes.r: Number of colours = 2^colour depth (2 to the power of the number of bits).
mistakes.w: Writing 2 x colour depth for the number of colours.

mistakes.r: A larger file comes from more pixels or more bits per pixel, which usually improves quality; always state which factor changed and what it does to quality and size.
mistakes.w: Saying a bigger file always means a better image.

mistakes.r: Read pixels left to right, row by row, starting at the top-left, unless told otherwise.
mistakes.w: Reading the binary image from the bottom up or column by column.

summary: You must know that a bitmap image is stored as a grid of pixels, each pixel represented by a binary number whose length is the colour depth, and that the image's resolution (number of pixels) and colour depth decide both quality and file size. You must also be able to describe metadata and calculate image file size (width x height x colour depth), then convert the units. It matters because every photo, screenshot and web graphic is stored this way and the trade-off between quality and size affects storage and downloads.

terms.d: The smallest element of a digital image; a single block of one colour (short for picture element).
An image stored as a grid of pixels, each with its own binary colour value.
The number of pixels in an image, usually written as width x height.
The number of bits used to represent the colour of each pixel.
Data about the data in a file, such as an image's width, height, colour depth, format and date created.
The amount of storage space a file uses, measured in bits, bytes or multiples of bytes.
A colour model in which each colour is made by mixing different amounts of red, green and blue light.
A table that links each binary code in an image to a colour.
A blocky appearance where individual pixels can be seen, caused by low resolution or enlarging an image.
Reducing the size of a file so it takes less storage or less time to transmit.
The part at the start of a file that holds its metadata.

worked.q: An image is 1200 pixels wide and 800 pixels high. It uses a colour depth of 24 bits. Calculate the file size of the image in megabytes (use 1 MB = 1000 kB = 1,000,000 bytes). Ignore metadata. [4 marks]
steps: Check: 960,000 x 3 bytes per pixel (24 bits = 3 bytes) = 2,880,000 bytes.

worked.q: A logo uses 40 different colours. (a) State the minimum colour depth needed. (b) The logo is 100 pixels by 50 pixels. Calculate the file size in bytes using this colour depth. [4 marks]
steps: (a) Test powers of 2: 2^5 = 32, which is fewer than 40; 2^6 = 64, which is enough. So 6 bits.

worked.ans: Model answer: A higher colour depth means more bits are used for each pixel, so the image can use far more colours (16.7 million instead of 256), giving smoother, more realistic colour. Because every pixel now needs 24 bits instead of 8 and the resolution is unchanged, the file size becomes three times larger, needing more storage.
worked.q: A photographer changes the settings of a camera from 8-bit colour to 24-bit colour but keeps the same resolution. Explain the effect on the image and the file size. [3 marks]
steps: Colour depth rises from 8 bits to 24 bits, so each pixel can show many more colours (2^24 = 16.7 million rather than 256).
So the picture has more accurate, smoother colours and better quality.
Each pixel needs 24 / 8 = 3 times as many bits, and the number of pixels is unchanged, so the file size is 3 times larger.
